entry.summary: No visa for tourism. With a chipped passport, e-gates at major airports authorise up to 180 days for tourism only.
entry.max_stay: Up to 180 days, but the officer sets the date: check the stamp or e-gate QR record.
entry.pre_arrival: Without e-gates: the online Multiple Immigration Form (FMM) and a QR code, shown on departure too. By land, get the passport stamped at the nearest immigration office and pay the fee.
entry.other: E-gates are for tourism only, adults only, and not when travelling with minors.

tourism.detail: Australians are listed among nationalities able to use Mexico's visitor entry, with the authorised stay determined by immigration at entry.
tourism.next: Check SRE/INM and keep the purpose consistent with tourism, meetings or unpaid activity.

meetings.route: Visitor for meetings and business exploration
meetings.detail: Meetings, market research and negotiations can fit visitor activity when there is no Mexican remuneration or employment.
meetings.next: Carry invitations and state who pays and where services occur.

conference.detail: Delegate attendance can be a visitor purpose; paid programme delivery is separate.
conference.next: Ask the organiser to state attendee versus speaker/trainer/performer.

unpaid-speaking.detail: Unpaid research, teaching or cultural participation can be supported by an institution, but the Mexican host should confirm whether a permit is required.
unpaid-speaking.next: Get the Spanish invitation to explain role, dates and expenses.

paid-speaking.route: INM-authorised employment or visitor with paid-activity permission
paid-speaking.detail: A Mexican employer normally obtains INM authorisation before the consular visa process; local remuneration is not covered by ordinary visitor entry.
paid-speaking.next: Have the employer begin the INM offer-of-employment route before advertising the tour.

book-launch.route: Visitor for rights; host/work route for paid launch
book-launch.detail: Publisher meetings can fit business; paid talks, readings, workshops, signings, merchandise and local sales need accurate Mexican classification.
book-launch.next: Separate author appearance, rights and retail.

ai-teaching.detail: University exchange and commercial training can use different routes; Spanish documentation may be required.
ai-teaching.next: Ask the institution to classify academic, unpaid and paid teaching.

remote-work.route: Temporary resident by economic solvency or other residence basis; no simple dedicated Mexican digital-nomad visa
remote-work.detail: Mexico is commonly used as a remote base, but visitor entry, tax residence and local work are separate. Temporary residence is a consular/residence process, not a guaranteed nomad permit.
remote-work.next: Confirm duration, foreign income, Mexican clients and tax position before basing remotely.

entrepreneur.route: Temporary/permanent residence with business or investment evidence
entrepreneur.detail: Founder activity can use residence and company pathways, subject to consular and INM requirements; owning a company does not automatically authorise local work.
entrepreneur.next: Choose the residence basis and operating role with a Mexican adviser.

trade.route: Visitor business route; local sales/import/service needs Mexican status
trade.detail: Meetings, sourcing and negotiation can be visitor activity; Mexican fulfilment, sales or installation may require work and customs approvals.
trade.next: Map importer, invoice, tax and on-site roles.

artist.route: Visitor only for non-remunerated activity or host-led work route
artist.detail: Paid performance, filming, exhibition and cultural work should be checked with the promoter and INM; visitor status does not cover local remuneration.
artist.next: Have the producer provide Spanish contracts, venue and payment details.

mixed-mission.route: Visitor first, INM/consular activation for local delivery
mixed-mission.detail: Mexico can absorb many purposes, but the local remuneration line must be explicit.
mixed-mission.next: Split tourism, meetings, foreign remote work and Mexican delivery before arrival.

filming.route: Ask the Embassy of Mexico, Yarralumla
filming.detail: No official statement on this activity was read. Easy entry isn't permission to work.
filming.next: Ask the Embassy of Mexico, Yarralumla which visa covers it, in writing.

research.route: Ask the Embassy of Mexico, Yarralumla
research.detail: No official statement on this activity was read. Easy entry isn't permission to work.
research.next: Ask the Embassy of Mexico, Yarralumla which visa covers it, in writing.

laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences, such as possession, use or trafficking are severe and include long prison sentences in local jails.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Smoking, including vaping, has been banned in all public places, including beaches, parks, hotels and restaurants. You may be fined or arrested.
laws.heading: Smoking

laws.rule: If you're considering entering into a surrogacy agreement, be aware that laws and regulations vary by state. While surrogacy is legal in some parts of Mexico, other areas have restrictions or outright bans, especially for foreign nationals. There is no legal framework to protect parents who pursue surrogacy in Mexico. laws.heading: Surrogacy

laws.rule: Property laws and time-share agreements can be complex. Before you buy or invest in property, do your research and get legal advice.
laws.heading: Property laws

laws.rule: Public displays of affection may attract negative attention. Same-sex relationships are legal, but the country is conservative. Same-sex marriages are recognised.
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ travellers

laws.rule: In Mexico, it's illegal to: conduct political activity, including demonstrations possess ancient Mexican artefacts or export them carry firearms or ammunition without a permit, including in Mexican waters drive a car without insurance fail to report a road accident. take photos and videos in restricted areas of Mexico City International Airport (AICM) urinate in public streets If you need a firearm permit, apply at a Mexican Embassy or Consulate before you arrive. You're responsible for any illegal items found in rented or borrowed vehicles. This applies even if you don't know they're there. If you're the victim of a crime and want to report the incident, do so immediately to the nearest bra
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: To drive a vehicle, you'll need a current Australian driver's licence. Foreign digital driver’s licences are not accepted.

This covers all forms of currency, not only cash. US dollars are widely accepted in holiday resort areas. You can't generally exchange Australian currency and traveller's cheques in Mexico. ATMs are widely available in cities and towns. Take care as credit card fraud occurs. Carry cash if you're travelling to rural areas.
